## Overview

The Efé are part-time hunter-gatherers living in the Ituri Rainforest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. They are one of three groups collectively named BaMbuti, alongside the Sua and Aka. The Efé occupy territory from the north to the southeast of the forest and are associated with the Lese people, with whom they cooperate and trade. They are Pygmies and are described as one of the shortest peoples in the world: men average 142 cm, while women tend to be about 5 cm shorter. Their economy combines hunting, gathering, honey collection, occasional wage labour, and exchange with Lese villagers. The Efé speak Lese, a Central Sudanic language.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

In the depths of the forest, the Efé are described as wearing little clothing because of the intense heat. During the *ima* celebration, girls who have reached menarche and have been secluded together in a hut are carried back into the village. The sources describe their feet as being wrapped in palm leaves during the period of seclusion, and state that they are carried when they need to go to an outhouse so that the sun does not touch them.

### Architecture

The Efé use leaf huts as shelter in the forest. Their camps are made on the outskirts of the forest near a Lese village for about seven months of the year, except during the best hunting season and honey season. Roadside villages created during Belgian colonial work projects differed significantly from the Efé’s forest villages.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do describe hunting tools and other everyday objects. Men hunt with spears or bows and arrows; arrows may be iron-tipped or poison-tipped according to the prey. Poison-tipped arrows are made after poisonous roots and vines are gathered, crushed, and turned into juice used to coat the arrow tips. The Efé also use dogs during hunts, including to drive animals from hiding places and chase wounded game. Through exchange with the Lese, they obtain iron, cloth, tobacco, marijuana, and other material goods.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They do describe the use of palm leaves during girls’ seclusion for the *ima* celebration, including wrapping the girls’ feet so that they do not touch the ground and so that the sun does not touch them.

## Music & performance

They mention the *ima* celebration, a religious ceremony shared with the Lese in which girls who have reached menarche and have been secluded in a hut together are carried back into the village.

The sources also mention a sound recording titled *The Pygmies of the Ituri Forest*, but the supplied material does not describe its contents or establish which musical practices belong specifically to the Efé. The sources therefore do not support naming instruments, musical forms, repertories, or performance contexts beyond the existence of this recording and the *ima* ceremony.

## Dance & theatre

The *ima* ceremony is described as a shared religious ceremony involving the return of girls from seclusion to the village, but no dance or theatrical form is identified.

## Festivals & rituals

They describe the *ima* celebration as a religious ceremony shared by the Efé and Lese. It concerns girls who have reached menarche and have been secluded together in a hut. One account describes the seclusion as lasting three months, while another describes it as lasting six months to a year. During this period, the girls’ feet are not allowed to touch the ground without being wrapped in palm leaves, and they must be carried to an outhouse so that the sun does not touch them. The seclusion is also said to make the girls fat, with palm oil and meat consumed in large quantities.

The sources describe other aspects of the Efé life cycle and family organization. Infants may be nursed by a woman other than their mother, and childcare is distributed among many people. The Efé ideal is marriage by sister exchange, although this occurs for only 40 per cent of men. There is no bridewealth and very little bride service. Marriage to anyone related to the bride or groom’s grandfathers is prohibited. Heritage is traced patrilineally, residence is generally patrilocal, and camps roughly follow the composition of a patriclan.

## Foodways

Efé foodways are based primarily on foraging, hunting, honey gathering, exchange, and occasional labour in Lese gardens. Men hunt and gather honey, while women gather forest foods, firewood, and water and prepare food. Forest foods include fruits, nuts, tubers, mushrooms, caterpillars, and termites. Men hunt monkeys, duikers, other antelope, water chevrotain, forest buffalo, and elephants. They use poison-tipped arrows for monkeys and iron-tipped arrows for duikers and other prey. Spears are used for large animals.

Honey gathering is an exclusively male task and takes place from June through September, although the honey season may last until November in a particularly plentiful season. Group hunts called *mota* involve between 4 and 30 men. Ambush hunts for duikers are called *ebaka* and are carried out from perches built in fruit trees.

The Efé trade meat and honey to the Lese for cassava, bananas, peanuts, rice, and other material goods. Meat obtained by the Efé accounts for over half of the meat eaten by the Lese. Efé women may help plant, harvest, and prepare food from Lese gardens in exchange for food. Efé men working in fields are usually paid with cooked food, though they may also receive marijuana or tobacco.

## Oral tradition & literature

Information about Efé religion is described as limited. The main source discussed in the supplied material is a collection of Bambuti legends that the author considered applicable to the pygmy groups of the Ituri forest, although the legends were collected from a net-hunting group rather than the Efé.

These legends are grouped into creation myths; legends of origin and tradition; legends concerning social relations; and legends concerning relations with the supernatural. Because the material does not specifically identify the legends as Efé, the sources do not support assigning particular stories to the Efé or naming a specifically Efé oral literature.

## Language & religion

The Efé speak Lese without a dialectical distinction from the Lese themselves. Lese is a Central Sudanic language spoken in the northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and is also occasionally known as Lissi or Efe. Efe has a separate ISO code, although Bahuchet states that it is not even a distinct dialect. Dialectical variation in Lese includes Dese and Karo. Lese is spoken in Mambasa Territory, Watsa Territory, and Irumu Territory.

The sources describe Efé religion as difficult to document because little information deals specifically with the Efé. Efé religious life is connected with that of the Lese, and some religious ceremonies are held in common, including the *ima* celebration.
